lesson.title: No Favorites: Understanding Uniform Distributions
lesson.summary: A uniform distribution has roughly equal frequency across its entire range, producing a flat histogram with no single peak standing out from the rest.
lesson.body:
A uniform distribution is flat: every value or interval across its range occurs with roughly the same frequency, so no single region of the graph stands out as a peak the way it does in unimodal or bimodal shapes. Instead of one tall cluster of bars, a histogram of uniform data looks like a row of bars all reaching about the same height, which makes uniform distributions easy to spot once you know what you are looking for, and easy to distinguish from every other shape covered in this unit, since it has essentially no discernible peak at all.

The clearest example of a uniform distribution is a single roll of a fair six-sided die. Each of the six outcomes, 1 through 6, has exactly the same probability of occurring, 1 out of 6, which is approximately 0.1667, or about 16.7 percent. If you rolled the die a very large number of times and made a histogram of the results, the six bars would all rise to nearly the same height, with only small random bumps from one bar to the next due to chance. No outcome is favored over any other, which is the defining property of a uniform distribution: equal likelihood, or equal frequency, across the whole set of possible values.

Uniform distributions also apply to continuous quantities, not just distinct outcomes like die faces. A spinner divided into equal wedges and spun to land anywhere along its circumference produces a value that is equally likely to fall in any equally sized arc, whether that arc is near the top, the side, or the bottom of the circle. Random number generators used in simulations are often built to produce uniform output over an interval, for instance generating any decimal between 0 and 1 with equal density, precisely so that no particular range of results is favored over another.

Uniform distributions have an unusual relationship to the ideas of mean, median, and mode covered later in this unit. Because every value is equally common, there is no single mode in the usual sense, or every value could be considered tied for the mode, so the concept of mode is not very informative here. The mean and median, however, still work normally and typically land at or very near the exact middle of the range, since the data is spread evenly and symmetrically on both sides of that midpoint. For the fair die, the mean of the six equally likely outcomes 1 through 6 is 3.5, the exact center of the range, even though 3.5 is not itself a possible outcome of any single roll.

Recognizing a uniform shape is useful mainly as a contrast to everything else in this unit: it tells you that no meaningful clustering is happening, so questions like "where is the peak" or "which values are typical" do not really apply, and your attention should shift instead to describing the range itself rather than searching for a center of concentration.
